news.title: Training gallery: Focused on Forest
Inside the life of Becky Spencer
news.body_en: We get to know Blues goalkeeper Becky Spencer better in our feature asking the Chelsea Women players about their early days in the game and their interests away from the pitch. Spencer is currently preparing for a huge game for Jamaica, who take on Costa Rica on Friday evening with a place at the 2027 Women's World Cup on the line. It is the latest chapter in a footballing journey that began 30 years ago now... I grew up in north-west London, a place called Harrow. I'm one of five, so I lived with three of my sisters and my brother. It was really nice. I had a good childhood. At what age did you first start playing football? I want to say five. Three of my sisters played football. I'm the youngest, and they all played in the same team. And I used to play for Wembley under-10s, but obviously they were in the seniors. So on a Saturday I would have my little seven-a-side games, and then on the Sunday I would go to the senior game. By the time they were retiring, football hadn't turned pro yet. This was in the nineties. So they kind of paved the way for me to be next. What was the name of your first grassroots team? How old were you when you first joined an academy? I grew up at Arsenal Academy. I was there from the age of nine until 22. Who would you say has been the biggest influence on your football career to date? I think it's just my family in general. I said that all of my sisters played. My brother also did play football, but my parents have obviously been around for all of that, so they took them to football and then they continued to take me to football afterwards. And you know, they put a lot of work in and a lot of sacrifice into making sure that I got to go for numerous years and travelling to places. What's your biggest career highlight to date? I've got quite a few to be honest, but I would say being at the World Cup with Jamaica, definitely. Who are your best friends in football? My friend Rosella Ayane. She's an old Chelsea player, and then I played at Tottenham for six years. She plays for Morocco, but yeah, we met at Tottenham. We always knew each other, but we met and we bonded straight away. And I'd say that she's one of my best friends. Also Drew Spence, another Chelsea player. I've known Drew for years and years, and then we just ended up playing in the same team throughout our careers, which you are lucky to do. We always take that for granted. Playing with your best mates is something that you never really think you're going to do. When you do, it's just like: ‘This is amazing’. Can you name your top three favourite players of all time? There’s a Valencia goalkeeper called Santiago Canizares. I used to love his style when I was younger. He used to have bleached blonde hair. When I was younger, I used to try and dress like him when I was playing and tuck my shirt in, wear his boots. I thought I’m nothing like him, but I just really enjoyed watching him. I'd say Rachel Yankee is one of my favourites. Also, I had the pleasure of playing with her, and she's now like one of my really really good friends. On and off the pitch, she's just one of my favourite people. And maybe Xavi from Barcelona. Definitely bought a shirt with his name on. It was one of those knock-off ones that you get on holiday. And I was like, 'I want his name on the back of mine' so my mum was like ‘let’s go to the shop’. By the time I got home, it was literally peeling off. When I was at the academy I had Spenny. That didn’t last long. Then I had 50 Spence. That didn’t carry on! What do you like to do most away from football? I’m quite introverted, so I like to have just time on my own. I’m a family person. I've got a little niece, she's so cute. So on days off, I'll go and see her and see if I can look after her for the day. On a Friday, we have this thing where my family still go to my parents' house. So we'll all congregate there on a Friday, have a meal, and just sit there and just chat about what everyone's been doing. Are you watching any TV series at the moment? I've just finished a couple, but I'm into reading at the moment. I’m reading Colleen Hoover, I’ve just finished Verity and I’m going onto Ugly Love now. If we looked at your Spotify playlist, who would be dominating your most-played artists? I'd say Olivia Dean. I put her album on and just let that play out at the moment What are your top three holiday destinations, either that you've been to already or you would like to go to? I would say Turks and Caicos. I went there just before the World Cup, lovely. I've just come back from Greece, so I went to Crete. That would be one of the best. And I'd say Jamaica. I haven't been to Jamaica on holiday, though, I always go to play or whatever. But I'll say Jamaica. I love going back there. If you had guests over for dinner, what would you cook for them? I’m not a very good cook! I'll try and do a seafood linguine. I’ll try! Garlic bread on the side, maybe a little side salad. Can you tell the fans something that they might not know about you? I made my professional debut when I was 14 at Arsenal. Sunderland away, my parents had dropped me to the training ground. The manager at the time was Vic Akers, he went and spoke to my parents, so they knew and then he called me. It was a freezing day up in Sunderland, not many people there. What's the best piece of advice you've ever received? I got some advice from Rachel Yankee. She said to me one time, ‘when you know, you know’. I think I've used it with loads of different things that I've done now. At my age, I think you've got to make some really important decisions, that’s made me also process things differently. It’s good advice. What does football mean to you? It means everything. I've never really been without it. I think when you are without it, even in the summer, you miss it. I think it's being around people. Also, having your own identity within a big group, it means everything because that's all I've ever known.

news.title: The Dave Sexton story
Made in Cobham: Heze Grimwade
news.body_en: Midfielder Heze Grimwade has grown up at Cobham, having joined Chelsea at the age of four. The Academy prospect reflects on the family support, hard work and determination that have helped shape his journey so far. From playing up an age group to spending extra hours working on his game, the Academy midfielder has always approached football with a clear sense of purpose. ‘It was always football. I have never wanted to do anything else, I’ve always been passionate. When I signed here I was so, so happy.’ Heze Grimwade’s unwavering focus on football has been shaped by a close-knit family environment, both at Cobham and at home. It’s an environment that has provided the support and structure for him to pursue his dreams from an early age. Born in Woolwich and growing up across south-east London, Grimwade has always been surrounded by his large family. The oldest of eight children, with two brothers and five sisters, he has grown up with the responsibility of setting an example for his younger siblings both on and off the pitch. Family has always been at the centre of his upbringing. Grimwade reveals that his parents made a conscious decision to structure their working lives around being present and homeschooling the 16-year-old and his siblings. That support has extended into his football, with his father being particularly influential in helping him pursue his ambitions. ‘My parents don’t work nine-to-five jobs because they want to be there for us,’ says Grimwade. ‘They have always been so involved with my career – my Dad is at every game and I’ve only missed one training session throughout my entire time with Chelsea. ‘Mum and Dad are always there and ready to support me. There have been sacrifices and I’m very grateful for what they’ve done for us.’ For Grimwade, football was always the ambition. He remembers attending sessions at Chelsea at the age of four and playing against much older children in his Sunday League matches at the weekend, even as a six-year-old. Having joined at such a young age, Chelsea has been a constant throughout almost all Grimwade’s life. He believes the club has played a significant role in shaping him, especially socially, having been homeschooled. The friendships the midfielder has developed at Cobham helped him develop and he credits the people around him with influencing his humour, confidence and personality. Grimwade has also become accustomed to playing above his age group. Having regularly played and training with older players since his early years, he has never placed too much importance on his age. ‘I don’t think about my age, I just focus on my ability and getting better every day. I don’t mind what type of match I play in, I just pray and ask God to guide me to make the right decisions, play with confidence and have enough energy to work for the whole game.’ That mentality has continued as he has progressed through the age groups, with the opportunity to train alongside older players providing further motivation. His biggest influences throughout his development at Chelsea has been the coaches who have worked with Grimwade across several age groups. Grimwade’s footballing development has involved various memorable moments over the years, but his favourite came against Bayern Munich in the KDB Cup back in 2025. He told us: ‘I missed a penalty earlier in that game and then we went down to ten men. We were drawing and then I scored a free-kick to win the game.’ Confidence has never been something he’s struggled with, and he emphasises that he approaches games with the intention to enjoy himself rather than allowing the occasions to overwhelm him. That confidence is also reflected in his approach to training. Grimwade’s routine extends to additional running and gym work often taking place on his off days. Away from football, Grimwade’s life is largely centred around family. His days are structured around training, extras and recovery, before returning home to spend time with his siblings. He is also someone who values routine, sticking to a bedtime of 7.30pm to allow him to recover fully and go again every day. There is a creative side to his family too, as his mother used to sing. Grimwade says: ‘All us kids can sing to a decent level, and our house is a house full of rhythm. We love music!’ For someone who has spent almost his entire life at Chelsea, his ambitions remain clear: to compete for the biggest honours in the game. The young Blue is proud of the journey that has brought him to this point but recognises there is still plenty of work to do. His focus remains on improving physically, developing his game and continuing to make the most of the opportunities around him. ‘I’m proud of myself and the journey so far, but I know there’s still a lot of work to do and I’m looking forward to it.’

news.title: N'Golo Kante's best Chelsea strikes!
news.body_en: On the day N'Golo Kante returns to Stamford Bridge to play in the Champions League, we have looked back at the goals the midfielder scored for Chelsea and picked out five of our favourites. Kante, now 35, currently plays his football in Turkey with Fenerbahce. They take on Shakhtar Donetsk in the league phase of the Champions League this evening, with the game in SW6 because the Ukrainian side are calling the Bridge home for their European football this term. During seven hugely successful and trophy-laden years at Chelsea between 2016 and 2023, Kante cemented his status as one of the world's top midfielders. While his game revolved more around cute positioning, destructive defensive work and bursts upfield than goalscoring, Kante still netted some spectacular strikes in blue. Here are five of the best, which are sure to bring back some happy memories... Kante’s first ever Blues goal is one to remember, with his sublime right-footed effort one of four Chelsea goals in our 4-0 win over the Red Devils. The Frenchman finished off a lovely move after Cesar Azpilicueta and Pedro combined well. The latter audaciously flicked the ball into Kante’s path before he danced through the visitors' defence and finished with aplomb. The midfielder cleverly slowed his run to latch onto an Eden Hazard cutback and thump a finish into the roof of the net against the champions Man City, on our way to a 2-0 Premier League victory in December 2018. A few weeks later, N'Golo somehow nutmegged three Tottenham players with a shot in the second leg of our League Cup semi-final tie with Tottenham. His sweet half-volley skipped into the net, with visiting keeper Paulo Gazzaniga the last to be bamboozled. Kante marked his return after injury by getting us back into the game against Liverpool with a stunning strike from the edge of the box. The Frenchman drifted in with the ball from the right, skipped past two Liverpool players before slamming his shot beyond Alisson and into the top corner. Kante exhibited his ability to find the corner of the goal throughout his Blues career, and nowhere was that more evident than with his low strike beyond Kasper Schmeichel with his weaker foot in a 3-0 win at the home of his former employers Leicester City.

news.title: OTD: Schalke v Chelsea | 25 November 2014
Terry Venables: A born leader remembered
news.body_en: Three years on from the sad passing of former Blues captain Terry Venables aged 80 on 25 November 2023, we remember why he will always have a place in the hearts of everyone at Chelsea. Terry Venables might be better known as the manager who almost led England to European Championship glory during a summer when football ‘came home’, but to an older generation of Chelsea fans, he will forever be the larger-than-life captain of Tommy Docherty’s Diamonds, the moniker bestowed upon the promising group of players coming through at Stamford Bridge in the early 1960s. It was quite the coup for the Blues to bring him to west London in the first place, as the Dagenham-born youngster was coveted by clubs throughout the capital during his school days. Chelsea finally secured the services of the boyhood Tottenham fan, just as they did with so many of the capital’s top talents around that time, thanks in no small part to the work of the larger-than-life club scout Jimmy Thompson and the clear pathway established between the Blues’ youth set-up and the first team. ‘Chelsea had a good name for bringing young kids through,’ Venables told Rick Glanvill for our official historian’s book Rhapsody in Blue. ‘Even as a kid you’re ambitious: you thought you’d get into the team at 17 or 18.’ He did just that, less than two years after arriving for his first day at the club in July 1958 alongside, among others, Peter Bonetti, Allan Harris, Bert Murray and Bobby Tambling. Harris and Murray were two he had struck up a firm friendship with on the schoolboy football scene; it was no coincidence the three of them ended up at the same club. His leadership qualities were spotted early on as he was made captain of a youth team which won back-to-back FA Youth Cups. It was during the first of those triumphs that Venables both started training with the first team and was given his senior Blues debut, which came in February 1960 when he was aged 17. Ted Drake’s side were beaten 4-2 by West Ham United at Upton Park, squandering a two-goal lead in the process. ‘I think it’s fair to say I could have had a better start to my career, with nothing I tried seeming to work for me,’ Venables wrote of the game in his autobiography, Born to Manage. He had started alongside Johnny Brooks, the former Tottenham Hotspur inside-forward who Venables had idolised and subsequently wished to emulate in terms of his composure, charisma and capability of splitting the opposition defence with a slide-rule pass. While that was the only first-team appearance Venables made that term, his attention switched back to the FA Youth Cup, which we won for the first time in 1960 before retaining it the following year. By this time, he had become a regular in the senior Blues set-up, although ‘senior’ may have been a stretch; Drake’s Ducklings, as our title-winning manager’s young charges were known, started the campaign with a side boasting an average age of 24, a number which had decreased to 22 by its conclusion. The inconsistency – some would say naivety – of youth was apparent by the goals for and against tallies, which read 98 and 100 respectively. It was clear, however, that the club had quite a player on our hands in the form of Venables, who took on the No4 shirt and looked to have all the qualities of a classic on-field general, dictating play from deep and directing players positionally. This was not a youngster lacking in confidence – he had, after all, displayed his showmanship over Christmas during his maiden full campaign in the first team by singing on stage at the Hammersmith Palais. An even younger Chelsea side, shorn of its talismanic frontman Jimmy Greaves, struggled during the 1961/62 season and it was largely an unhappy campaign for Venables as he played only 12 matches. There was the highlight of his first-ever goal in senior football, which came in a heavy defeat at Cardiff City, but after featuring in Drake’s final game as Blues boss, replacement Tommy Docherty called upon Venables only three times as the club dropped down into the Second Division. The following campaign saw the transition from Drake’s Ducklings to Docherty’s Diamonds, with Venables one of the major players as we immediately bounced back to the top flight, playing every minute of our 42 league matches that term. A penalty on the final day – the first of eight successful conversions from the spot in the league during his Blues career – in a handsome victory over Portsmouth secured our return to Division One. Aided by his promotion to spot-kick duties, Venables became a regular name on the score sheet for the remainder of his time at the club, but far more noteworthy at that time was his contribution towards dressing-room harmony. During the 1963/64 season he became club captain, a natural role for a player who was always the life and soul. Nearly all of his team-mates from that time spoke fondly of a man who loved a prank but, more than anything, always had the backs of those he led out onto the pitch every Saturday. ‘Terry was a leader right from the start of his career,’ said team-mate Barry Bridges, who came through during the same era. ‘When he was captain I suppose he was only 19 or 20, but he did more to lead the team than the manager. He was the guvnor on the pitch and it was no surprise to see what he went on to achieve as a football manager himself.’ Venables’ first full season as skipper, in 1964/65, was arguably the best of his time here. Not only did it include his only trophy won as a Blue, it also saw his club form recognised at international level. As a result of the two caps won for the senior side during the space of 49 days during the winter of 1964, he became the first man to be capped by England in schoolboy, youth, amateur, Under-23 and full internationals, although he would never play for his country again. After scoring on the opening day of the campaign against Wolverhampton Wanderers, Venables added two more in consecutive games against Leeds and Arsenal which confirmed us as genuine title challengers. A penalty in the first leg of our League Cup final against Leicester City helped secure the club’s first-ever triumph in a major cup competition, but our bid for a domestic Treble came unstuck in the closing weeks. With Venables and Docherty often at loggerheads – two jocular fellows who loved nothing more than to be the centre of attention – things came to a head with the infamous Blackpool incident, when the skipper was one of eight players sent home from an away trip due to breaking curfew. Though he was one of those to return for the final-day loss at Blackpool, the damage had already been done – both to our title hopes and the relationship between captain and manager, despite a brief reconciliation. Winning the League Cup had gained us entry to the Fairs Cup the following season and the European stage seemed to suit Venables down to the ground. He scored a famous hat-trick against Roma in the opening round, which included a goal which would have been replayed time and time again had it occurred in the modern era. When a free-kick was awarded to the Blues, Venables made a song and dance of counting out 10 yards and then, having reached the wall, spun around to receive the pass before finishing with aplomb. ‘We worked things like that out beforehand,’ he said of that cheeky goal. ‘We were non-stop talking about football, like in the cafe in Fulham Broadway, for hours after training. Talking about what you could do, how you could get better.’ The hat-trick came at the end of a run of eight goals in nine games to begin that season, but he would not score again until March and the underlying problems with Docherty came to a head after our tepid FA Cup semi-final defeat to Sheffield Wednesday, when Venables was among those singled out for criticism by the manager. Unfortunately, the damage this time was irreparable. The beginning of the end came in the away dressing room at the Nou Camp ahead of a Fairs Cup semi-final against Barcelona, when Docherty introduced the players to new signing Charlie Cooke. The story goes, as told by the manager, that Venners decided to test the new boy by throwing the ball to him; Cooke promptly caught it on his instep before juggling the ball, taking it on his neck and then flicking it back to Venables. That game in Catalonia would be his last in Chelsea blue. ‘I think I knew then,’ Venables conceded years later. ‘I got the hint when he was juggling the ball in the corner! Things had got to a bad stage. I didn’t understand at the time, but if someone’s got to go, it’s always the player. I’d always wanted to play for Chelsea and I loved it so much I wanted to be there all my career. I didn’t want to go.’ He left just a fortnight later, joining Tottenham Hotspur for a fee of £80,000 and a year later he was part of the side, along with Greaves, which beat their old team-mates in the FA Cup final. Venables represented two more London clubs, Queens Park Rangers – losing an FA Cup quarter-final against the Blues in 1970 as we went on to lift the trophy for the first time – and Crystal Palace, before bringing down the curtain on his playing career in 1974 and embarking on a new chapter in football as a coach. His last two clubs on the pitch were the first two of his managerial career, which hit new heights in 1984 when he took over at Barcelona. ‘El Tel’, as he was dubbed, brought a hard-nosed 4-4-2 to the Nou Camp, where he was ably assisted by his old Chelsea team-mate Allan Harris, and won La Liga in 1984/85. However, they lost the European Cup final against Steaua Bucharest in Seville the following season. He came home to London to manage Tottenham in 1987 and added another FA Cup triumph to the one from his playing days with the Lilywhites and he was also the last Spurs boss to beat Chelsea, in 1990, before our famous 12-year unbeaten run against our rivals. Following this, Venables was given the honour of leading England at a major championship on home soil, as he was appointed manager two years out from the European Championship. His popular Three Lions side captured the hearts and imagination of the country as they reached the semi-finals of Euro 96 before suffering penalty shootout heartache against Germany. Having left England at the end of the tournament, brief spells managing Australia, Crystal Palace, Middlesbrough and Leeds followed before Venables stepped away from football. The lure of assisting Steve McClaren during his ill-fated tenure in charge of England briefly pulled him back into the game, but both left their jobs with the FA following the failure to qualify for Euro 2008. However, it is for the ability, determination and leadership he demonstrated on the Stamford Bridge pitch that he will forever be remembered at Chelsea.

news.title: Emmanuel Emegha on doing ‘anything to win’ and why Reece James is the ‘best captain’
news.body_en: Emmanuel Emegha announced himself to Chelsea supporters with a brilliant goal against Leeds United on Saturday, offering a glimpse of the qualities he is eager to bring to the Blues. Emegha’s performance and goal was one of the few bright spots of an otherwise disappointing afternoon at Stamford Bridge. The striker’s pace, power and natural finishing ability were all on display, with the Dutchman marking his full Blues debut by opening his account for the club. In a career that has already seen him move from his native Netherlands to Belgium, Austria, France and now England, Emegha has always risen to meet the level required of him. He expects to do the same here, as he told our official matchday programme for the Leeds game. ‘That’s why I know that at Chelsea I can and I will also do it,’ said Emegha. ‘Every player is different. There are some players, you buy them and straight away they are… boom! Me, I always need some time to adapt, and I’ve had a lot of injuries. ‘Now I’m happy that I’m over it and I do everything for my body to stay as fit as possible. I want to stay like this because playing for a big club, you cannot be having these injuries, injuries, injuries. It will not work. ‘I’m a winner, I’m a fighter,’ added Emegha. ‘I would do anything to win. If I need to block a ball with the front of my face, I will do it. I’m quick, I know how to make runs in behind, and I know that I can be a nightmare for all the defenders.’ With his height and pace, it appears Emegha possesses the characteristics required to perform in the Premier League. Despite that, he acknowledged training at Cobham every day and playing in English football has been a real step up from what he has known before. ‘I’m in a room full of such talented players, it’s not normal!’ he explained. ‘Before coming, I knew that I could expect a high level, but I didn’t know that it would be so crazy high. But I’m enjoying it. I’m getting better. I’m learning every single day.’ Emegha’s adaptation to life at Chelsea has been aided by the support network around him. The human touch off the pitch can make a big difference on it, and the 23-year-old has felt warmth and care from day one. He also made a point of singling out the skipper for praise. ‘I don’t think that I’ve worked at a club with so many nice people,’ said Emegha. ‘To be honest, since my first day here, even in the kitchen, the way that they take care of us is next level. ‘I also want to say that Reece James is the best captain I’ve ever had in my whole life. I came to this club and he made me feel comfortable. Reece James… he has won it all, he has seen it all, but he’s still so caring. I don’t know how it is for other players, but Joao [Pedro] said it too. One day we had a meeting and he said the same thing. ‘For me, Reece is the example of a leader. He would come to me and make sure that I felt good. If I had a tough training session, he would come to me and tell me, “It’s normal. Tomorrow is a new day. Forget it and move on.” If I missed an open chance in training, it would be easy to say, “Oh, come on!” But Reece… he thought, “Oh, come on!” but he said, “No, come on. Next one, next one!” And he wasn’t even in my team that session! He made me feel so good.’ And if James's message is to keep looking forward and take the next opportunity, Emegha is certainly intent on doing just that. news.title: Bjorn and Bronze talk leadership and bouncing back stronger in We Are Chelsea
news.body_en: The latest episode of the We Are Chelsea podcast features defensive duo Nathalie Bjorn and Lucy Bronze joining us to chat and discuss a wide range of subjects, including their individual styles of leadership and how last season inspired them to come back stronger than ever in 2026/27. The pair are part of a Chelsea Women team enjoying a great campaign so far, sitting two points clear at the top of the Women’s Super League table and on course for direct qualification to the knockout stages of the UEFA Women’s Champions League. The Blues remain undefeated in all competitions with 13 wins from 18 games, having scored 39 goals to just seven conceded, while keeping clean sheets in our last four consecutive fixtures, including vital wins over Manchester City and Paris Saint-Germain. That form was just one of the subjects they discuss in the latest episode of the We Are Chelsea podcast, which you can watch in full below. When asked about that impressive form, Bjorn and Bronze both pointed to the lessons learned during a disappointing 2025/26 season – following a hugely successful debut campaign for head coach Sonia Bompastor – as crucial to coming back stronger than ever. ‘From when Sonia first came in and we had this whole season we went unbeaten and everything is good, and then you have a second year that is worse for us,’ explained Bjorn. ‘Then it is all about how you come out from that, what makes you stronger as a group. Obviously none of us is happy with that season, but also it was good value for us – as a group, as players – to be like: “okay, we need to do this better, we need to have better intensity, we need to do this, this and this”. ‘I think that actually helped us get the team together and be able to perform like this.’ Bronze added: ‘Sometimes transitions are a lot harder, especially our first season everyone was like “wow”. ‘But it’s kind of like a honeymoon phase of everything’s going really well and then suddenly something doesn’t go as well and you don’t have as much to fall back on because it’s new territory, under Sonia especially, and we had to figure a lot of things out. ‘I think that’s what you saw in the second year, which normally you would see in the first season. But I think it worked out well because we still knew as a group that the first season gave us so much confidence that we were a good team, we could win and we could do well. So last year it was like this isn’t forever, this is just us repositioning ourselves, figuring ourselves out to be that team again and to be even better.’ As two of the most experienced members of this Chelsea squad, with well over 200 international caps between them, Bjorn and Bronze both take on vice-captain roles for the Blues, alongside skipper Erin Cuthbert. However, as they explained when asked about the other’s strengths, they have very different approaches to leadership, a variety both feel is important to have within such a diverse squad. Bjorn highlighted the way Bronze leads by example, saying: ‘Obviously Lucy, the way she puts in standards in the sessions, in the games, she’s mentally strong and her physicality. ‘If it’s running down the line and you do a tackle or whatever, she always puts the standards really high. That also shows that people take after her, want to do the same, I think it’s impressive.’ Bronze responded: ‘She’s the person who brings people together. It’s so important for a team. ‘It’s easy sometimes to drive a standard, but keeping these players in the right place and making sure everyone’s always together and there’s not a person dropping off, Nat’s the one who’s always bringing them back together, bringing everyone together, always positive, always a good vibe. ‘So we’ve got a good mix of personalities and things that we bring. The perfect leader doesn’t exist, you need to lean on each other. It’s a big group of players with so many personalities, we have to be able to lean on each other and not think we know everything.’ You can watch Bjorn and Bronze discussing those subjects and many more by watching the latest episode of the We Are Chelsea podcast in full above.

news.title: Seven memorable moments against Nottingham Forest
news.body_en: Chelsea and Nottingham Forest's Premier League history dates back to the competition's very first campaign in 1992/93, and since then there have been plenty of games for us to enjoy against the Reds. As well as league meetings in that time, we have faced Forest on several occasions in domestic cup competitions, and our selection of memorable moments includes some of those. The Blues will be trying to add to this list on Friday evening when we travel to the City Ground, and to whet the appetite we take a trip down memory line... Nottingham Forest had only played four matches back in the top flight after promotion when they came to the Bridge, and Gianfranco Zola gave them a quick lesson on how tough the challenge can be in the Premier League. Very quick, in fact, as there were just 25 seconds on the clock when the Italian opened the scoring on our way to a 2-1 victory. Chelsea won the third of our eight FA Cups in 2000, but we were challenged along the way by Forest. This game was almost a personal challenge for Zola, who had one brilliant chip cleared off the line before being flagged offside when tapping in a team-mate's already goal-bound effort. He made amends when we regrouped in the second half, setting up Frank Leboeuf’s opening goal as we won 2-0 and progressed to the fifth round. Chelsea’s 2017/18 Carabao Cup campaign kicked off against Forest at Stamford Bridge with an emphatic 5-1 win on Willy Caballero’s debut. However, it was Michy Batshuayi who starred. The striker only gave us glimpses of his potential with the Blues, but when he did it tended to be memorable. This wasn’t quite up there with his title-winning goal at West Bromwich Albion, but his first – and only – Chelsea hat-trick was a high point. Spanish duo Alvaro Morata and Cesc Fabregas were both playing their last game for Chelsea when we hosted Nottingham Forest in the 2018/19 FA Cup third round. The latter wore the captain’s armband on his 500th match in English football, but also had a penalty saved. That left it for Morata to save the day on his farewell appearance, scoring twice in the second half for a 2-0 Blues win. There were three games left in the Premier League season when Chelsea travelled to the City Ground in 2023/24 with both sides desperate for the points, Forest in a bid to avoid relegation and the Blues in the race for Europe. We took an early lead but were trailing heading into the last 10 minutes, before Raheem Sterling curled into the bottom corner. Two minutes later, a peach of a Reece James cross allowed Nicolas Jackson to head in and give us a dramatic 3-2 victory. The City Ground hosted our last Premier League game in 2024/25, and what a day it was. Effectively a head-to-head contest in the race for UEFA Champions League qualification, a tense match was decided shortly after half-time when Levi Colwill turned in Pedro Neto’s pass for the only goal of the game. Cue wild celebrations in the away end, Chelsea were back in the Champions League. A few months later, we triumphed in emphatic fashion on the banks of the Trent, emerging 3-0 victors with all the goals scored after the break. The highlight was the opener, nodded into the net by Josh Acheampong for his very first senior Chelsea goal. The grin on his face said it all!

news.body_en: We ask Lola Brown some quickfire questions to get to know the 19-year-old, so impressive in Chelsea Women's draw with Liverpool, a bit better… What is your favourite pre-match hype song? PGA Division 1 report: Chelsea Women Under-18s 10-2 Birmingham City
news.body_en: Chelsea Women’s Under-18s, who play in Division 1 of the PGA Women’s Under-21 League, produced a dominant display at Kingsmeadow on Sunday, scoring ten goals against Birmingham City. Despite conceding inside the opening minute, the Blues responded impressively, netting three times shortly before the break and then adding seven more goals after the interval. Seven different Chelsea players got on the scoresheet, with the result extending our unbeaten start to the Division 1 campaign. The performance also featured contributions from several members of our Under-16s squad. The visitors made a dream start, scoring just 22 seconds after kick-off. A misplaced pass allowed Birmingham to move forward quickly and, after working the ball into the penalty area, they found the net from close range. Chelsea responded positively and began to establish control of possession, with our pressure rewarded in the 38th minute. Keira Johnson set the ball back for Tess Finn, who drove beyond the Birmingham defence before finishing from inside the penalty area to equalise. Four minutes later, the Blues went ahead. Nelly Las and Johnson combined on the right before the latter's cross was cut out. The clearance fell to Maria Mayers on the edge of the area, and she took a touch before firing into the top-left corner and celebrating in style (top). There was still time for another before the break. Straight from kick-off, Las played the ball forward to Ella Abayomi, whose pass across the edge of the penalty area found Gabi Storey. The defender struck first time, sending an excellent effort beyond the goalkeeper to make it 3-1. Chelsea maintained their attacking momentum in the second half, with Abayomi adding her name to the scoresheet five minutes after the restart. Las delivered from the right and Abayomi finished confidently inside the penalty area. Jahmya Putman made it five in the 61st minute. Chloe Sarwie released Aysia Matabaro down the left, and the winger reached the byline before cutting the ball back for Putman to finish first time. A Birmingham defender then turned Sarwie's inswinging corner into her own net in the 66th minute, before Abayomi scored her second two minutes later. Matabaro again provided the delivery, picking out the forward inside the box for a composed finish. Storey then claimed her second of the afternoon in the 75th minute, meeting Las's pass with a shot that flew past the goalkeeper. Birmingham pulled one back a minute later after a long clearance caused problems for the Chelsea defence, allowing their striker to run through and score. The Blues responded with two more goals. Matabaro drove through the penalty area before finishing with her right foot in the 79th minute, following Maria Mayers' pass. The scoring was completed in the 88th minute. Mayers regained possession and found Matabaro on the left, whose cross reached Las. She controlled before shooting, with a deflection helping the ball find the top corner to complete the 10-goal haul. The victory means Chelsea remain unbeaten in PGA Division 1 after four matches, collecting ten points from a possible 12 as we head into the international break. The Blues now take a break from domestic action, with several members of the squad set to represent their countries at Under-17 and Under-19 level. Chelsea return to PGA Division 1 action on Wednesday 9 December, when we travel to face Bristol City. news.title: Bompastor: Lola Brown’s mentality is ‘unbelievable’
news.body_en: Sonia Bompastor was full of praise for Lola Brown after her impressive Chelsea cameo in our Women’s Super League draw with Liverpool. The 19-year-old came off the bench and had a big impact on the left flank, causing trouble for the hosts and creating a chance for Sjoeke Nusken that forced a fantastic save from Khiara Keating in the Liverpool goal. Bompastor said that while competition for places is currently high, Brown’s mentality has been ‘unbelievable’ as she looks to earn more time on the pitch. ‘Lola didn't get many minutes [previously],’ Bompastor said. ‘The competition is high in this squad with many experienced players. ‘What she's been doing since the summer has been good, really good. Her mentality is unbelievable; she always works hard and puts a big effort on the pitch. ‘The quality she brings with the ball, she's a really confident player. I just felt from what I could observe in this game, she was probably the right profile to come on as the left wing-back. ‘I think we wanted to create more with crosses. She did well, we couldn't convert some of the crosses that she put in the box, but again from everyone I had available on the bench, she was probably the right profile to replace Sandy Baltimore.’ Brown has been called up to England Women’s Under-23s squad for the forthcoming international break, with matches against Belgium and Portugal on the agenda.

news.title: Romeo Lavia: This is not the moment to panic
news.body_en: Romeo Lavia says Chelsea must use the pain of yesterday's 4-1 defeat to Leeds United as fuel to provoke a strong reaction, starting with our trip to Nottingham Forest next week. The Blues started brightly at Stamford Bridge and deservedly took the lead midway through the first half when Emmanuel Emegha marked his full debut with a clinical left-footed finish. However, Noah Okafor levelled just three minutes later, and after Dominic Calvert-Lewin converted from the penalty spot early in the second half, further strikes from Okafor and Brenden Aaronson condemned us to a heavy home defeat. Lavia did not hide his frustration at letting a promising start slip away, though he was clear that the dressing room will remain calm and united. ‘Everyone is very angry and disappointed,’ said Lavia. ‘At home this is never the way you want to finish a game. We let them back in the game when we shouldn’t have. This is something we will analyse and get better at. ‘When we won games, when we lost games, we always said that no matter what, it’s a process,’ Lavia added. ‘With these types of results, it feels like the end of the world, but we are not going to ring the bell now to say it’s a panic moment. Not at all. We are very confident as a team. We know where we want to get to. ‘This hurts, it needs to hurt so it provokes a reaction from the team, and this is definitely going to help us for the next game on Friday.’ Lavia also acknowledged the disappointment felt by supporters inside Stamford Bridge. The Belgian emphasised that the players take full accountability for falling short of the standards expected. ‘Of course, this is Chelsea Football Club, a club that wins trophies and is expected at the highest level every time,’ Lavia said. ‘At home it hurts times ten. You always want to give the fans what they deserve, and that wasn’t the case. We understand it and we take full responsibility.’

news.title: Alonso: We need to be tougher to recover from setbacks
news.body_en: Xabi Alonso has identified the key area his Chelsea team needs to improve as he reflects on a disappointing afternoon at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, believing we have to learn to take a 'punch' and bounce back stronger. Despite taking the lead against Leeds United through Emmanuel Emegha’s first goal for the club, the Blues never recovered after the visitors responded with a quick equaliser, as three second-half goals condemned us to a 4-1 defeat in the Premier League. Our manager admitted it was a particularly tough result to take given the rivalry between the two clubs, as he shared the supporters’ frustration at the final whistle. ‘I understand their disappointment for sure, and we share that with them,’ he said. ‘The only thing we can do is work, try to give our best to turn it back and to do much better. ‘We were disappointed, the fans were disappointed. We were disappointed because the expectations from them are high and we feel sorry for them. We need to go through this together and to find solutions together. ‘Now, for sure, it's not the easiest moment. We're in a fragile moment, but we need to work together and stick together, because there’s still such a long way to go.’ In order to find those solutions, Alonso wants his team to be more resilient to bounce back from on-pitch setbacks, an area he feels we lacked both in Saturday’s game and the loss away at Sunderland before the international break. That is along with better handling opponents like those, who take a physical and direct approach to the game, especially given it is something he expects us to face on a regular basis in the Premier League. ‘We need to find solutions for sure, because there will be setbacks during any game, and we have to be tougher and to be able to go through that and to know that there’s still so long to play. It's something mandatory in this competition. ‘I felt that probably we are in a fragile moment mentally, in our confidence. When we received a punch we didn't recover from that strong or tough enough. That was my feeling. ‘We need to deal with that because this is the demand of the Premier League. Not just yesterday. When we go on Friday against Forest, this will happen to them. There were moments that we were not competing at the level required. We need to know that's mandatory in this competition, because we will face teams with that demand again. ‘But the physicality, the duels, that is not the only explanation. We could do better in a football way – not giving the ball away, trying to progress a little bit more, choosing better options. But as well, the physicality and the mentality are parts we can do better. ‘Our job is to try to find solutions, to work on that, to have experiences – bad experiences like yesterday, and hopefully we will have good ones when we can – and overcome even during the game a difficult moment, because this is football and for sure that will happen. In the progression, in the process that I often talk about, this is a very important topic.’ Alonso now has just under a week to work with his team at Cobham to try to rectify those issues before our next fixture, when we travel to Nottingham Forest for the Premier League’s Friday evening kick-off.

news.title: Bronze frustrated after dominant display against Liverpool
news.body_en: Lucy Bronze admitted she and her Chelsea team-mates were frustrated after being unable to convert their dominance over Liverpool into a win in the Women’s Super League. The 0-0 draw on Saturday leaves the Blues two points clear at the top of the table, but Manchester City will be in action on Sunday with a chance to reclaim top spot before the international break. It was a performance full of control for Sonia Bompastor’s side, especially in the second half, but Liverpool keeper Khiara Keating was in inspired form, with a save from Sjoeke Nusken the pick of her numerous saves. After coming away with a point from St Helens Stadium, Bronze said the team have to score more goals from the chances they are creating, a theme that has troubled them at times already this year. ‘Yeah, [it was frustrating],’ Bronze said. ‘Especially after the second half. ‘First half was a bit more even, although we created some good chances, they had one or two as well, Hannah had some good saves - more than she usually has. ‘But then the second half, I think we completely dominated the game. It just felt like Nusken's chance at the end, probably on another day, that goes in the back of the net, and a few other chances as well. Obviously Khiara Keating had a great game.' Bronze acknowledged that Saturday's draw with Liverpool was reflective of several matches already this season and recognised the Blues expect more. She continued: 'The end product was there a few times, but the goalkeeper saved it. We need to create more, we need to do more, score more goals. 'I think that's been the story of our season - not scoring as many goals in certain games as we should do. Thinking of the draws we've had with Aston Villa and Everton. Same today. All games, again we should be winning and scoring more goals.’

news.title: OTD: Chelsea 3-2 Bolton | 22 November 1995
Bompastor: We must be more clinical and find a better balance
news.body_en: Sonia Bompastor insists she is happy with the way her Chelsea side are performing, but says they must find a better balance between being solid defensively and creating more goals as they continue to challenge on multiple fronts. The Blues came out 1-0 winners against Paris Saint-Germain in the UEFA Women’s Champions League in midweek thanks to a late goal from Veerle Buurman. However, they were unable to find another strike to put Liverpool to the sword, despite an incredibly dominant second-half performance. Bompastor says that while her team needs to be more ruthless and clinical, the overall level of play has been impressive. ‘I think right now we need to find a better balance between the defensive aspects,’ Bompastor said in her press conference after the draw against Liverpool. ‘I'm really happy also with the way we build up no matter the opponent; if they come and man-mark, if they leave us a little bit more space. ‘The things we need to improve are in the creation-finishing phase: making sure we create as much as possible in the games and we are clinical and ruthless in the box when we have those opportunities.’ Bompastor said her side have been working on a number of aspects of their attacking play as they look to increase the number of goals scored, but added that sometimes these things do take time to come to fruition. ‘I think we were dominant in the second half,’ she added. ‘We have been working a lot on the final third, in the box, details around the timings of the runs, the positions in the box and the mentality around how we want to attack the box as well. ‘When I talk about being ruthless, clinical, it's the desire to be first on the ball. All these things we have been working on, and we will keep working on. ‘It takes a lot of time sometimes to get those connections right, and to be able to be in the right positions. But we need to keep working because sometimes the difference can be when you start to lose a little bit of confidence in that box, it can change things a little bit. ‘So we need to stay confident and make sure we do everything we can under our control to turn these things around. ‘I'm really happy with a lot of things we are doing right now. When you have ambitions, when you want to win titles, you need to make sure to find the right balance between being strong defensively but also being able to score goals. ‘So yeah, we need to be that team, and I would like to have a better balance in terms of being able to score more.’

Alonso updates on Caicedo’s game-changing injury
news.body_en: Xabi Alonso feels the injury suffered by Moises Caicedo against Leeds United played a big part in changing the momentum of the game in the visitors’ favour, but knows Chelsea need to respond to those setbacks better in the future. The Blues suffered a 4-1 defeat to Leeds at Stamford Bridge on Saturday afternoon, in our first game since the international break. Caicedo started the game wearing the captain’s armband, but a collision left him in some pain, and eventually brought an early end to his game when the Ecuadorian was replaced by Jordan Henderson in the 22nd minute. ‘It's a knock and we need to wait until tomorrow to see how he is,’ said Alonso, when asked if Caicedo’s injury was serious after the game. ‘He was in pain and let's see how bad it is.’ Although we took the lead shortly after that enforced change, through Emmanuel Emegha’s first Chelsea goal, Leeds responded to level the scores almost immediately and we struggled to recover control of the game after the double setbacks of Caicedo’s injury and Noah Okafor’s goal. ‘What went wrong was after their equaliser, after the change with Moi, we lost completely the momentum,’ continued the Blues manager. ‘Until then we were doing okay. I think that we were creating, playing a lot on the pitch. We were coming out from the pressure, but from that moment, they started believing, we started not believing. ‘After that, we never got the good feeling mentally in any moment and we were not able to come out from the pressure, we didn't get close to their goal, so it completely changed the game.’ Responding to those setbacks is an area our manager knows we need to improve, something he sees as a joint responsibility among himself and his squad. ‘I feel that as a team, as a collective, together we need to support each other,’ Alonso added. ‘Today, together, we need to find solutions to do better because this will happen. ‘On the pitch, they need to go through those moments to say: "Okay, we are still in the game, we still have many minutes to play and the game is not over”. ‘The game still had so many minutes to play and we felt that we didn't recover that good momentum.’

news.title: Bompastor provides Mayra Ramirez and Manaka Matsukubo injury update
news.body_en: Sonia Bompastor has given an update on Mayra Ramirez and Manaka Matsukubo, with the Chelsea duo eyeing a return from injury. Ramirez missed almost the entire 2025-26 season after undergoing surgery on a hamstring problem, but has been targeting a return to first-team action. After being spotted back with the squad following the win against Paris Saint-Germain in the UEFA Women’s Champions League in midweek, Bompastor was asked how close Ramirez is to making a return for the Blues - but the manager said patience will be key before the striker returns. ‘Yeah, so Mayra is back in the country,’ Bompastor said. ‘I think we are working with her on fitness to make sure she is back with us on the pitch. ‘For now, she is still rehabbing, and she has not been part of the training sessions with the squad. ‘So we need to take the international break also to keep assessing her and see how she evolves, and I will have an update - probably a better update - after the international break. 'But yeah, she missed a lot of the season, the beginning of the season, so she needs time to build up again.' Matsukubo, meanwhile, missed the clash against PSG and was an unused substitute during the Women’s Super League draw against Liverpool. Bompastor said that while the attacker was available to play, she preferred to use other options off the bench following the injury. ‘Yeah, Manaka got a pain in her glute, so we decided to have her in the squad [rather than starting] today,’ Bompastor said. ‘Probably she still wasn't 100 per cent. From what I could observe, I felt other profiles would have been better in this game to come in.’

news.title: Match report: Chelsea 1-4 Leeds
news.body_en: Chelsea succumbed to defeat to Leeds United in the Premier League despite Emmanuel Emegha marking his full debut with his first goal for the club. It was initially the Blues who looked to be the strongest side when we took control of possession midway through the first half, and then the lead when Emegha smashed in the first goal of his Chelsea career left-footed, after good work by Morgan Rogers to tee him up. It was not to last, though, as a couple of minutes later a Leeds long-ball gave them the opportunity to level the scores through Noah Okafor. It remained all square at half-time, but early in the second half the visitors were awarded a penalty when a shot struck Rogers high on the arm, allowing Dominic Calvert-Lewin to take the lead from the spot. Leeds extended their advantage when Okafor got his second of the game from close range after a long-throw was only half cleared and then, as we tried to find a way back into the game, Brendan Aaronson got another for Leeds on the counter late on, sealing Chelsea's fate. Xabi Alonso made four changes to his team, with Emmanuel Emegha leading the attack on his first start for Chelsea, supported by Estevao Willian, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers. Romea Lavia and Moises Caicedo continued in midfield, the latter as captain. Behind them, Josh Acheampong returned to the defence alongside Levi Colwill, Wesley Fofana and Pep Chavarria, with Emiliano Martinez back in goal for the Blues. As always when these two old rivals meet, both sets of supporters were making plenty of noise as this game kicked off at Stamford Bridge. On the pitch, it was a slightly cagey opening, as the two teams probed for openings. Emegha set out his stall early on his full Chelsea debut, giving the home fans a taste of what he is all about by mixing it up with the Leeds centre-backs and making his physical presence felt. It was the home side who gradually began to control proceedings, with Acheampong and Estevao in particular linking up well on our right flank at the start. Rogers was trying to find his range from just outside the box with a couple of efforts, but neither keeper had been tested after 15 minutes. However, when Leeds managed to produce their first spell of pressure in the Chelsea half, it almost gave them the opening goal, when Calvert-Lewin got his head on the end of James Justin’s cross, with Martinez relieved to see it come back off the crossbar. Earlier, Caicedo had needed lengthy treatment on his back following a collision in the air, and eventually he was unable to continue, handing the captain’s armband to Colwill as he was replaced by Jordan Henderson midway through the first half. Shortly afterwards, the Blues put that set-back behind us by taking the lead. Rogers got the better of Justin to bring the ball down, surge past Muharemovic in the middle and feed Emegha down the channel. The striker steadied himself and unleashed a venomous left-foot shot to beat Trafford at his near post. It was quite the introduction to the Bridge supporters. Unfortunately, our lead lasted less than three minutes, as Leeds hit straight back. A long ball caused problems as it dropped out of the sky and broke for Okafor in a dangerous position. He carried the ball into the box and was able to divert his finish into the bottom corner to level the scores. The game continued fairly evenly balanced after those two quick goals, but it was Leeds who came closest when Calvert-Lewin flicked a cross wide and headed too close to a grateful Martinez. Muharemovic did get the ball in the net as Leeds' high balls proved dangerous, but it was ruled out for a clear offside, meaning the teams went in for the half-time break level. There was a slightly chaotic start to the second half amidst a series of appeals from both teams, largely ignored by referee Michael Oliver. That was until a shot ricocheted off Rogers in the box five minutes in. Leeds appealed, the penalty was given, and Martinez had no chance as Calvert-Lewin fired into the bottom corner. Rogers tried to hit straight back after we fell behind, but his shot was too close to Trafford to trouble the keeper, and as we attempted to regroup and push back, we fell further behind. It all came from a long throw which was only cleared as far as the edge of the box. Rogers got a foot to Ampadu’s cross but couldn’t prevent it reaching Okafor, who struck into the top corner on the half-volley, from too close for Martinez to react. Alonso turned to his bench in response as Pedro Neto and Danny Welbeck were introduced to our attack, soon followed onto the pitch by Malo Gusto and Geovany Quenda. It seemed to have the desired effect as we regained control of the ball and began to pen Leeds back deep into their own half with 20 minutes remaining, but with a two-goal deficit there was plenty of work to do if Chelsea were to salvage anything from this game. The Blues worked hard for little reward, though. With their lead secured, Leeds dug in stubbornly to prevent us from carving out clear chances. Instead it was the visitors who scored again on the counter, through substitute Brendan Aaronson in added time. Chelsea are in action early next weekend, travelling away to Nottingham Forest for the Premier League's Friday evening kick-off on 27 November. Kick-off is at 8pm. news.title: 'Lola Brown is showing a lot of quality'
'We need more belief in front of goal'
Match report: Liverpool 0-0 Chelsea
news.body_en: Chelsea were held to a draw away at Liverpool in the Women's Super League, with the Blues dominant but unable to force a winner. The result pushed us a further point clear at the top of the table, with Manchester City in action on Sunday afternoon. The Blues were on top early in the first half before Liverpool forced their way into the game before the break. However, after half-time it was all Chelsea as Sonia Bompastor's side went in search of a winner. While the Blues will undoubtedly be frustrated not to come away with all three points, they maintained their unbeaten start to the season. Bompastor made two alterations from the 1-0 UEFA Women’s Champions League win over Paris Saint-Germain, with Lucy Bronze replacing Nathalie Bjorn in defence. Elsewhere, Sjoeke Nusken came in for Aggie Beever-Jones. After a cautious opening 10 minutes, Hannah Hampton was the first goalkeeper called into action. However, it was a fairly tame header that proved an easy stop for our No.1. Moments later came the first real opening for the Blues as Ellie Carpenter raced down the right flank, pushing into the area before looking for Sandy Baltimore with a cut-back. It would have been a certain goal for Baltimore, but the pass was cut out by a Liverpool defender. Keira Walsh then had an effort from just inside the area, but her curled attempt flew wide of the post. The Blues kept the pressure on, with Lexi Potter flashing an effort wide from outside the area. Liverpool's first chance of real note came after 24 minutes, with a blocked clearance allowing Vivien Endemann to get on the ball in the area. However, her lay-off to Natalia Ramos was dragged well wide by the Spanish star. We continued to press forward with Walsh seeing a shot blocked after a short corner, before Alyssa Thompson came close to opening the scoring. The 22-year-old broke forward before firing in a left-footed shot that was pushed over the bar by Khiara Keating. Fuka Nagano then forced a great stop from Hampton. The keeper was alert as the ball dropped to the Liverpool attacker, stopping a fierce effort before gathering the ball at the second attempt. Ramos then came close for the visitors with a free-kick, whipping the ball just over the bar. Both teams went in search of an opener before the break, with Endemann pouncing on a loose pass before firing a shot harmlessly over the bar for the hosts. Ramos then had a shot from outside the box which Hampton did well to parry before collecting. The Blues attacked quickly with five minutes left as Baltimore was found in space down the left, but she couldn't find the back of the net with Keating closing down the angle in the Liverpool goal - as the score remained level at the break. We came out strong to start again, with Carpenter forcing Keating into an intervention from a cross, while Walsh showed quick feet before having a shot blocked. Walsh then forced another save from Keating, her high shot palmed over the bar. From the corner, Veerle Buurman almost poked an effort home but saw her attempt blocked. Bompastor did not leave it long to make a change, with Lola Brown making her way onto the pitch around 10 minutes into the second half, replacing Baltimore. Brown had an instant impact, playing a nice one-two before delivering a cross into the centre, where Thompson just couldn't get over the ball to put her header on target. Carpenter quickly earned another corner for the Blues, flying down the right before firing in a cross which almost deceived Keating. With just over 20 minutes remaining, Brown fired in another dangerous cross; this time Nusken saw a powerful volley pushed behind by the Liverpool keeper. As we entered the final quarter of the contest, Brown fired in another dangerous cross, this time Nusken saw a powerful volley pushed behind by Keating. Walsh then had a snapshot which seemed to take everyone by surprise before rolling just wide. Following a scramble in the area, Broze did well to find Walsh again on the right side of the area, but her shot was again well-saved by Keating. Potter then had an opportunity, attempting to place an effort past Keating but seeing her shot stopped. Bompastor made one last throw of the dice in the final 10 minutes as Beever-Jones, Erin Cuthbert and Giulia Dragoni were introduced, with Thompson, Kaptein and Nusken making way. A stop-start finish to the game ensued, with the Blues unable to create any more clear-cut chances before referee Ben Speedie blew up for full-time. We remain unbeaten and go two points clear at the top of the Women’s Super League, but will head into the international break in second place if Manchester City beat Tottenham on Sunday. This was the last fixture before the final international break of the year. news.title: Xabi Alonso on Emmanuel Emegha selection for Leeds clash
news.body_en: Xabi Alonso believes Emmanuel Emegha is ready to take his opportunity against Leeds United, as the Dutch forward prepares to make his first start for the Blues. Chelsea return to Stamford Bridge following the two-week international break, with Alonso determined to see his side get back to winning ways against Leeds. The forward made his Blues debut in our Carabao Cup clash against Liverpool and earned his first Premier League minutes against Sunderland before the international break, and now Alonso has included him from the off for the first time this afternoon. Explaining his selection, Alonso said: 'We have seen a lot from him, but he needed to build his fitness because he had picked up a few injuries. Now he's been training for a long time, he's played some minutes, he's been patiently working hard and now he's got the chance to start. 'And today, hopefully, he has a good game and he's feeling good.' With Emegha joined in attack by Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Estevao Willian, Alonso is hoping to see plenty of creativity from his side. However, the Blues manager has stressed that maintaining the right balance between attack and defence will be crucial against Leeds. The boss continued: 'Our attacking players need to be ready to defend, ready to have this solidity that is needed in these kind of games. 'But as well, we need creativity, we need to be a threat in the last third. With these players we can have it, but we need to play a complete game.'

news.title: Confirmed Chelsea line up vs Leeds
news.body_en: Xabi Alonso has made four changes to his starting line-up for today’s fixture against Leeds United, with Emmanuel Emegha coming in to make his full Chelsea debut in attack. Emegha looks set to lead the line as the central striker, making his first start for the Blues after coming off the bench against Sunderland and Liverpool. He will be supported by Estevao Willian, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, as Pedro Neto and Jordan Henderson drop out. Romea Lavia and Moises Caicedo continue in midfield, the latter as captain. Behind them, Josh Acheampong returns to the defence alongside Levi Colwill, Wesley Fofana and Pep Chavarria. Emiliano Martinez is back in goal for the Blues for his first appearance since suffering a fractured jaw at Everton. Mike Penders and Marco Palestra are the other two players to make way, with both among the substitutes this afternoon. Leeds have made one change to the team which beat Tottenham Hotspur 1-0 before the international break, as Noah Okafor relaces Lukas Nmecha in their front three. They are captained by former Chelsea youngster Ethan Ampadu.
